body: Indian sector bull runs often get most of their return from multiple expansion, not earnings. When that happens, the next decade's return is borrowed. Examples: capital goods (2003–Jan 2008 at P/E 40–80x, then about 14 years to regain the index peak); real estate in 2007 (DLF and the realty index fell 80–90% and stayed down to ~2020); FMCG/consumer in 2019–21 (55–75x for HUL and Nestle, followed by roughly five years of flat-to-weak relative returns as multiples compressed); specialty chemicals at the 2021 China+1 peak (50–80x, then a 40–60% drawdown in many names through 2023–25 destocking); defence PSUs in 2023–25 (forward P/E ~2x historical); EMS in 2024–25 (60–120x). Common early signals at the top: the sector's P/E at more than 1.5–2x its own 10-year median, IPO and QIP supply surging in the theme, new entrants announcing capacity, and earnings upgrades slowing while prices still rise. Then a disclosure or accounting scare (Kaynes 2025) or a margin miss triggers the de-rating. Lesson: split past returns into earnings growth and multiple change, and assume the multiple mean-reverts over 5–10 years unless RoCE or growth has structurally changed.

data.lesson: Decompose returns into EPS growth vs P/E change; a doubled multiple is a loan from future returns.

title: Sector re-ratings end when multiples double while earnings only grow
